title: French ex-President Nicolas Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to be tried next year
description: Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for c
body: Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy. The pair deny any wrongdoing.Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence – of which six months were suspended – over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail – two of them suspended – and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the €50m (£43m) in payments continued after he became president. Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.At the time, Sarkozy was said to have stated: the "truth is finally coming out", but officials found the retraction to be "insincere" and a new investigation was launched into the "Save Sarko" file – the nickname the alleged perpetrators had used for the operation, according to French media.So the former head of state and his wife, an Italian-born former supermodel and singer, will now face the charge of "criminal conspiracy to commit fraud as part of an organised group and receiving stolen goods related to witness tampering". They deny any wrongdoing.

schema.headline: French ex-President Nicolas Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to be tried next year

title: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner
description: Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Can
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney. "We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress. "I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala. He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians."I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration. The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster, external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's, external support for Trump. They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media., externalCritch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel."Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

schema.headline: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner

title: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
description: A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities
body: A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom."We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said."The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari."Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

schema.headline: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say

title: Villavicencio car bomb: More than 20 injured in attack in Colombian city
description: Three weeks ago, three adults and a baby were killed in a car bomb attack near army barracks  in Tolima province. And earlier on Monday, drones droppe
body: Three weeks ago, three adults and a baby were killed in a car bomb attack near army barracks  in Tolima province. And earlier on Monday, drones dropped explosives on the police headquarters in the northern city of Cúcuta.  The car bomb in Villavicencio went off on Monday evening - the eve of the 10th anniversary of the signing of a peace deal between the government and left-wing rebels of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc), Colombia's largest guerrilla group.Following the signing of the deal, thousands of left-wing rebel fighters laid down their arms.However, a significant number of Farc members, who did not agree with the deal, refused to disarm and joined dissident groups instead. While forced displacement, child recruitment and the numbers of attacks on security forces dropped in the aftermath of the deal, there has been an upsurge in recent years driven by dissident Farc factions and criminal groups fighting for control of drug trafficking, illegal mining and extortion rackets.Colombia's first left-wing president, who was in power from August 2022 to August 2026, tried to negotiate with these armed groups as part of what he called his "total peace" strategy. However, the talks stalled and collapsed with several of the criminal groups violating ceasefires they had agreed to observe.De la Espriella was elected on a promise to crack down on "narcoterrorism" and has been scathing about his predecessor's approach. He has also been critical of the 2016 agreement, calling it a "false peace".In a post on X, uploaded shortly before news of the car bomb in Villavicencio spread, he referred to the peace deal as a "mess", describing it as a "waste of public resources" and the "cause behind Colombia's ruin". Former President Juan Manuel Santos and Rodrigo Londoño - the two men who signed the peace deal on behalf of the Colombian government and the Farc respectively - defended it in an interview with BBC Mundo ahead of the anniversary. Santos said that De la Espriella was "totally wrong" to call it a "false peace"."He wants to use, or has bought into that cynical and mistaken theory that the violence we see today is the result of the peace deal, when the exact opposite is the case," Santos said, arguing that the problem lies with the lack of implementation of the agreement.

schema.headline: Villavicencio car bomb: More than 20 injured in attack in Colombian city

title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
description: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after German reports that Russia is preparing to launch a nuclear
body: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after German reports that Russia is preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said such reports were "not new, yet they remain no less shocking", and a government spokesman said the reports were being taken "very seriously".Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had not seen the reports but dismissed stories citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper Süddeutscher Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites. Asked about the reports, the Nato secretary general told a press conference in Berlin alongside Merz: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."The Western defensive alliance had a variety of response options, said Rutte."When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary."Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, told the Handeslblatt newspaper that having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario".Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Bleddyn Bowen, co-director of the Space Research Centre at Durham University, said that exploding a nuclear weapon in space would have "massive infrastructural effects" as there were now more than 15,000 active satellites. But he told the BBC's Today programme that "the effect of these weapons would be extremely indiscriminate and also take out a lot of Russia's own space infrastructure".Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.In 2024 the US accused Russia of developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation. "Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

schema.headline: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports

title: Saurav Das CJP: Indian government has 'lost the plot' says 'cockroach' party leader after being barred from UK flight
description: One of the leaders of India's "cockroach" movement has said the Delhi government has "completely lost the plot" after he was stopped from leaving the
body: One of the leaders of India's "cockroach" movement has said the Delhi government has "completely lost the plot" after he was stopped from leaving the country for the UK. Saurav Das said he was meant to board a flight on Tuesday morning but was told by immigration officers his passport had been "flagged" because of discrepancies involving his date of birth.In an interview with the BBC, Das said there were no discrepancies in his documents, accusing the Indian government of using cheap tactics to stop activists from travelling and speaking on issues that matter to young people. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.Saurav told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme the incident showed the government was "scared"."They are scared of the cockroach movement. They're scared of young people asking them questions because they have never had to deal with a generation that wants to ask questions so head on. So that jitters them."By not allowing him to travel, he said the government had lowered India's stature in the world. "It's international news that I am unable to travel to the UK," he said. "And this shows Prime Minister Modi in such poor light."It's a way to harass, to target activists, young voices in India by the Modi government."Das said he had been invited by the Oxford Union, as well as universities including Cambridge and Edinburgh, to speak about the movement.Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), wrote: "The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country."On Tuesday, the London School of Economics Student Union's Amnesty International Unit, a student-led charity group, shared a post on Instagram saying that an event featuring Das had been "indefinitely postponed".Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi. Das insisted the CJP would continue protesting, but it did not want to be a political party "as of today"."It's a long haul. We are not here for a short time. We are looking at India in the next 10 to 20 years. How do we develop India into a better country? That is the vision that we want to carry forward."Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.Additional reporting by Cherylann Mollan.

schema.headline: Saurav Das CJP: Indian government has 'lost the plot' says 'cockroach' party leader after being barred from UK flight

title: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
description: At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials a
body: At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military.The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza.Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas.Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City.Several other people were reportedly seriously injured in the strike.The Israeli military said Abu Nahel had "possessed extensive institutional knowledge" about Hamas's internal security service - which is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting infrastructure and rooting out informants - and that his death constituted "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities".It also alleged that he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war and that it killed him "to remove the threat he posed".Gaza's interior ministry said Abu Nahel's killing followed what it described as the internal security service's "important achievements in combating gangs collaborating with the occupation [Israel] and operating in areas under the control of its military".Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to thousands of shelters for displaced families.The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.On Tuesday, the health ministry warned that there had been a rapid rise in cases of meningitis, with 272 reported in October - about eight times the usual monthly average.Fifteen deaths had been attributed to the infection so far this year, including five reported between August and October, it said.Israeli military body Cogat said on Monday it was "working to provide a dedicated humanitarian response" and that a newly approved package of pumps, generators, water tankers and medical equipment had been presented at a meeting with UN agencies.The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

schema.headline: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza

title: South Africa femicide: Night-time curfews and street patrols after women murdered in Ekurhuleni
description: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African policeImage source, Family handoutImage caption, Okuhle's body was fou
body: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African policeImage source, Family handoutImage caption, Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering studentByNomsa MasekoThuthuka Zondi and Eleanor Smallwood BBC World ServiceReporting fromEkurhuleniTuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured."When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten."It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBCImage caption, Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's deathOkuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.It is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years as police had stopped releasing this breakdown until now.There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South AfricaThe BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confront widespread violence against womenIn response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.But in places like Kokstad, as well as Kempton Park, in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested."It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received. The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South AfricaAccording to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change."I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBCImage caption, Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers."With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBCImage caption, Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap herKgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her."Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBCImage caption, Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistlesIn September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" -  after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later.It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.Zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group."We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBCImage caption, Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killedFollowing her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.Wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone."This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

schema.headline: South Africa femicide: Night-time curfews and street patrols after women murdered in Ekurhuleni

title: Pope Francis' diary reveals claims he saw the devil three times
description: Pope Francis claimed he saw the devil three times over the course of his life, as well as the "gates of hell", according to new extracts from his priv
body: Pope Francis claimed he saw the devil three times over the course of his life, as well as the "gates of hell", according to new extracts from his private diary.In The Private Diary of Pope Francis, published on Tuesday, a 2021 entry lists the late pontiff as having three visions of the devil: once from a car, another "in the choir loft" during Mass, and a third during a meeting with Vatican officials."I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote, recalling one of the visions.In the diary, written from 1992 to 2024, he also expresses regret over his 2018 visit to Chile, when he was criticised for defending a bishop who was accused of covering up sexual abuse committed by a priest.Francis, who led the Catholic Church for 12 years until his death in 2025, later apologised and summoned the country's bishops to Rome, where they all offered to resign."Devastated because of the situation in Chile," Francis wrote in a 2021 entry."It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious."Of his encounters, which Francis interpreted as meetings with the devil, he said he could not forget the devil's "menacing" eyes."He looked at me with flaming eyes... more intense than the previous one. They were like flashes of fire," he wrote of his second vision that he said happened inside a Carmelite chapel while he was archbishop of Buenos Aires.He said the devil's presence intruded on his journeys, including during the visit to Chile amid the clerical sexual abuse scandal, and a meeting a few days after he had returned to Rome."I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant, possessing everything," he wrote, adding that "the Lord gave me the chance to free myself from these encounters".

schema.headline: Pope Francis' diary reveals claims he saw the devil three times

title: Bangladesh's ex-PM Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return on 16 December
description: Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced
body: Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule. She denies the charges.Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms."Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a ​request for comment. In April, ​the ministry said it was ⁠examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties".Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution."Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said in a statement.The choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement.Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh.Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile.The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster.The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister.But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return.Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so."I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster.Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka.India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a new government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster.But nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September.Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi. The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.

schema.headline: Bangladesh's ex-PM Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return on 16 December

title: On the streets with the French Black Block ultra left protesters
description: 'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra leftFigure caption, Watch: The BBC's Katya Adler speaks to protesters
body: 'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra leftFigure caption, Watch: The BBC's Katya Adler speaks to protesters taking part in recent demonstrationsByKatya AdlerEurope EditorFrance is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.This Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present.President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he says, is to bring down the French Republic.That's quite a claim – and one that needs examining.The unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The left in France blames the centre and right for the cost-of-living crisis that's making French people so upset and angry. They blame the hard left for fomenting violence (which they deny). While the nationalist right pledges, if elected, it will return order and security to France's streets.So, who exactly are these "ultra-left" groups Macron speaks of? And how organised and dangerous are they?It's infamously hard to speak to members of the radical left. They don't much like what they call mainstream media. We're viewed as part of an establishment many of them despise.My best bet was to head out into the protests and try to approach people dressed in all black and ski masks or balaclavas (worn, they say, to hide their identity from police). It's a quasi-uniform associated with left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block.You see them at demos all over Europe. In France, they tend to appear from city side streets, as daytime protests are dying down, dusk is falling and riot police begin to emerge in full force.Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBCImage caption, The BBC's Katya Adler talking to a protester French intelligence drastically underestimated the outpouring of anger, looting and destruction following protests last month. More than 1,000 police officers were reportedly injured, young protesters had bones broken and two reportedly lost a hand in altercations with police armed with stun grenades. Le Monde newspaper has an article, external it is constantly updating to investigate a rising number of reports of protester injuries. The French Insurers Federation estimates damages to shops and private property on 17 October alone - the day of the biggest riots - came to around €207m (£175.5m).Since then, the French authorities are trying to tightly manage demos. Police presence is heavy. Protesters say heavy handed.Towards the end of one of the protests this month, we saw would-be rioters vastly outnumbered, glass bottles and homemade paint bombs at the ready to throw at police. They were no match for the batons, stun grenades and tear gas the officers had to hand.Image source, ReutersImage caption, French police pepper spraying protesters during a demonstration by French high school and university students in Paris earlier this monthAs we were being forcefully kettled in by police, I tried to talk to would-be rioters. Few wanted to engage but I then met 18-year-old Nas (not his real name) and friends. They would only speak to me if they could hide their identity. This was to avoid police detection, they said.Milling, you could say provocatively, by baton-at-the-ready police – they seemed to fit a radical-left rioter stereotype."How can you justify the violence?" I ask them."Without violence, you don't achieve anything," one of them tells me. "It's the only way to get our voices heard.""We come from an area with a bad reputation. Our schools are a mess. Our teachers quit. You need qualifications to get a decent job. There is supposed to be equality in France. We won't give up our fight."These young men, we discover, come from the sprawling housing estates common on French city outskirts - the banlieues - associated with deprivation, unrest and second or third generation immigrant families.They weren't politicised or organised by the radical left, they insisted. Just angry.Image source, Lee Durant/BBCImage caption, Left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block, tend to dress in all black, wearing ski masks or balaclavasEarlier, I had spotted two hard-left student activists, standing masked on top of a bus shelter, above the thronging crowd of protesters waving banners sporting the red anarchist sign and the symbol for the Antifa (anti-fascist) movement.I put it to them that France has a proud tradition and respect for the right to protest but that the country has been horrified by the violence it's seen over the last weeks.They were keen to downplay the rioting but - again – would only speak if they could remain anonymous."Violence ends up reflecting badly on our movements. We don't like it. But what's a smashed shop window compared to police using stun guns on protesting school kids? Also, people [in France] are regularly going cold and hungry. They're losing faith in this society."How could they believe violence would bring about a juster society, I wondered?They shrug off my question. In France, these days, the real violence is state violence, they say.Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBCImage caption, Some protesters don't support the Black Block's violence but say the state's violence is worseFrench intelligence estimates there are 5,000 "ultra-left" activists in the country.Anticapitalist Starflix (that's his codename) counts himself as one of them. The 17-year-old is also a member of the violent Black Block movement. We'd arranged to meet on the edge of the protest, by a narrow canal.Fearful about being apprehended by police, he asked to remain anonymous.He showed me a couple of homemade paint-bombs - eggshells filled with paint and sealed with medical tape that he throws at police officers. He carries them in his rucksack, wrapped in a royal blue Italia football shirt."We throw the paint bombs at the visors on riot police helmets, so they have to lift them up in order to see and that makes them suffer their own tear gas that they've sprayed at us," he tells me."We pick up stones and rocks too. Anything we find on the streets of Paris, to throw."I put it to him that he and others in the Black Block are causing a lot of problems on French streets: damaging businesses, hurting police officers, destroying the demos for peaceful protesters. What is he trying to achieve?As he's under 18, his parents give us permission to speak to him. They share his politics, Starflix tells me, but not all rioters - masked and dressed in black as he is - do."The Black Block isn't a single organisation. It's a technique. Some of us use violence to get government reform. I want to bring about a revolution."Other people are opportunists who use anonymity to steal things. When we all wear the same clothes, it makes it harder for police to identify us."When I ask if he is scared he might get hurt or arrested, he admits he is but says what frightens him more is the thought that society might not change.Social media plays a huge role in the riots. Starflix tells me he and his friends use Signal and Telegram to arrange to meet at protests.Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBCImage caption, "The Black Block isn't a single organisation," says protester StarflixThere are numerous websites and Instagram profiles, mainly hosted by left-wing organisations, offering tips for protesters and rioters, such as: keep your phone at home so police can't track you, cover your face to avoid being identified and emulate martial arts expert Bruce Lee and "be like water" - appearing and disappearing into crowds. That's advice passed on by the Hong Kong protesters eight years ago.While not formally organising the protests or violence with these posts, could the fact groups host this information online be viewed as a kind of incitement or manipulation of youngsters whose feelings are running so high in France?All the young rioters I spoke to insist they are not being herded or directed, but is there something bigger behind what's happening?Image source, Lee Durant/BBCImage caption, Ultra-left protesters spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymityIt takes our team a long time, but they manage to find a seasoned activist with the Black Block who would speak to us. I put to him Macron's assertion that the ultra left has organised groups that aim to bring down the French Republic. Is that true?"It's totally false of the authorities to say we are all organised. And the intelligence services know it," the activist scoffs. "It's a manipulation of the French public to make them think there is an enemy within.""Basically, people turn up to a protest, get dressed in black and do their own thing. The uniting factor is rage and not just in France. You see the same rage [in protests] in Italy, Germany, Spain. It's exploding by itself."I ask if the anti-capitalist presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his France Unbowed party (LFI) are somehow linked to the violence. They are present at most protests, supporters handing out campaign pamphlets to the chanting crowds.But the activist denies this, telling me Mélenchon is "a capitalist because he's part of the system". He says the LFI and the trade unions try to "calm" unrest, while he believes things need to be "stepped up a notch".Why had he decided to talk to us, I ask - does he want to collapse the French government?"I just want to say we don't love violence. I don't want to destroy France. We want to destroy a system that is a capitalist system, of course, but to change the society in a way that we think will be better for the most people, for more people. "More and more find it hard to make ends meet. In the countryside, people can't even afford to fill their tank with petrol."You have to leave the city, heading out into the gloriously autumnal French countryside, to meet some of the more organised, hardcore elements of the ultra left.Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBCImage caption, Limoges Town Hall, allegedly damaged by protesters, has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be inThis is a world of eco activism and known saboteurs. One man remains in police custody linked to the fire during protests at Limoges Town Hall last month. The devastated, yet somehow still elegant, 19th century building has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in. An acrid smell still hangs in the air one month on.The 34-year-old arson suspect, who insists he's innocent, comes from a hamlet near Limoges, known for its anarchist, environmentalist community. His father, a fellow activist, is also known to French intelligence. We approached the father and the suspect's lawyer for comment. They didn't want to speak.Instead, we met a 39-year-old father of one, a local full-time ultra-left activist for more than two decades. Like the other individuals we spoke to for this investigation, he would only talk to us on condition he could remain anonymous."We were all shocked by the [town hall] fire – even as we watched it happen in front of us - but it's our duty to take action," he tells me."I can't leave this world to my son in the state that it's in. Look how military vehicles and brute force are used by the state against our young students."It's amazing the people haven't taken up arms against them. Do we need a policeman killed in order for the state to listen?"How can you say that, I want to know?"As a child, I was educated with French values – liberty, equality, fraternity - but when I look at the social injustice in the world now, I'm disgusted. As a father, I can't let this go on. If I have to, I would take a bullet to protect the youth of this country."These are dangerous-sounding words - but the radical left doesn't appear to be big, armed or united enough to seriously threaten France.Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBCImage caption, Upcoming presidential elections offer a crossroad, with polls predicting a run-off between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc MélenchonWe repeatedly approached French intelligence. They didn't want to comment. A sign perhaps of the huge sensitivity of the current situation, especially with France hurtling towards an extremely charged presidential election.But Michel Klein, a recently retired former police commissioner, told me he didn't think the radical left posed a serious threat to the French state."I believe there is a will from the radical left and the anarchists to try and destroy the Republic but they obviously don't have the means to do it," he told me.He sees no risk of civil war in France (a possibility you hear some in the country discuss these days) but he identified a rising risk of clashes between far-left and far-right groups ahead of the presidential election.Polls currently predict a run-off in the vote between nationalist candidate Marine Le Pen and anticapitalist Mélenchon.Far-right vigilante groups have begun appearing on the edge of protests in a number of cities across France to "protect French streets", they say.The popular hard-left presidential candidate Mélenchon attends most demos, his supporters handing political pamphlets to the chanting crowds, but he denies any links with violence.France is so polarised, there's little sign next year's presidential vote will calm things. This turbulent mix of left and right, social and political unrest, feels like a perfect storm.

schema.headline: On the streets with the French Black Block ultra left protesters

title: DR Congo conflict: Army seeks missing aircraft as FRN rebels claim to shoot down plane
description: The Democratic Republic of Congo military says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.Th
body: The Democratic Republic of Congo military says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a plane of the same type that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive.On Tuesday, the FRN said the plane they had shot down was a Cessna 208, which had been "converted into a light attack aircraft" enabling it "to carry and launch precision-guided bombs and missiles".Its wreckage now lies 10km (6 miles) from Minembwe, a rebel statement said.The BBC has not independently verified the rebel claim, or whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one the rebels say they shot down.Uganda's military on Monday denied any involvement.A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X said: "UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company."The statement did not identify the company or explain what penalty had been imposed.Gen Kainerugaba later posted that "no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]". Uganda's denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane's wreckage.In the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man's identity.He and the alleged South African pilot are said to be the only other survivors. South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a "mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy"."Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC," deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet.In 2022, DR Congo's army blamed M23 rebels, who are now part of the FRN, of shooting down a UN helicopter in which eight people died. The rebels denied it.The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels.In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas.The rebels control large areas of eastern DR Congo, including the major city of Goma, after major territorial advances last year.Aid agencies say the violence is increasingly disrupting healthcare services.Over the weekend, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières said fighting in North Kivu had forced some of its teams to temporarily suspend outreach activities.The fighting has also affected the response to the Ebola outbreak, with many health workers trapped, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.

schema.headline: DR Congo conflict: Army seeks missing aircraft as FRN rebels claim to shoot down plane

title: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book
description: Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.
body: Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes.""Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation. "We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy"."These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade. Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.If you have been affected by the issues in this story help and support can be found at BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book

title: Syria land mine casualties soar, two years after war
description: Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when th
body: Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang."Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.Unwittingly, the children had triggered a landmine.The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.Alaa's father said demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe."Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC.The dangers are reflected in a sharp rise in casualties across Syria.A total of 1,602 people were killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2025 alone, an increase of more than 50% on the previous year, according to the Landmine Monitor report, published by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines on Tuesday.Only Myanmar, with 1,891 casualties, recorded more.The report attributes the rise in Syria partly to the large-scale return of refugees and internally displaced people following Assad's overthrow."When you look at population movement, a couple of months later you see an increase of incidents in these areas, because that's exactly where people go and start to use the fields again," Atkins said.More than 60% of casualties recorded by the world's largest landmine clearance charity, the Halo Trust, involve farming, agriculture or shepherding, according to its Syria programme manager, Simon Jackson."They're not going to wait for the government or for organisations like us to come and tell them that everything is safe and clear," he told the BBC. "People are taking risks out of desperation."Since Assad's fall on 8 December 2024, Unmas has recorded at least 1,556 incidents in Syria involving explosive ordnance.They have caused 2,701 casualties: 935 people killed and 1,766 injured. Children account for 995 of those victims, or about 37%.But the toll is likely to be higher, with experts estimating that overall casualties could be under-reported by 25-50%.For many of those who survive, the consequences are devastating and permanent.Majid Abdul Rahman, 27, was travelling in a car in the Ghouta region on the outskirts of Damascus in March 2025 when it struck an explosive device. The vehicle filled with smoke and he felt a pain in his leg.More than a year later, Majid has difficulty walking and has been unable to return to work, leaving him struggling to provide for his family.The danger has continued into this month, with at least 20 people killed and more than 40 injured by explosive ordnance in November.In one of the worst recorded incidents, an explosion in a school courtyard in Hasakah on 4 November killed a 12-year-old and injured 19 others. And on Monday, a 13-year-old boy was killed when an unexploded cluster munition detonated in southern Daraa province.The threat is also holding back Syria's economic recovery. Contaminated farmland cannot be safely cultivated, while people collecting scrap metal or trying to salvage materials from abandoned areas also risk triggering explosions.The Syrian Ministry of Defence says since the end of 2024 its teams have found and dealt with more than 315,000 mines and unexploded munitions.But no nationwide survey has established how much land remains contaminated, making it difficult to assess the full scale of the problem."We're in a bit of a black hole," Atkins said.And with the extent of contamination still largely unknown, the war continues to claim victims two years after it ended.Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus

schema.headline: Syria land mine casualties soar, two years after war

title: South African court convicts Zimbabwean of trying to fight in Russia-Ukraine war
description: A Zimbabwean national has been convicted by a court in South Africa of planning to go to fight in Ukraine.The country has strict laws which restrict u
body: A Zimbabwean national has been convicted by a court in South Africa of planning to go to fight in Ukraine.The country has strict laws which restrict unauthorised involvement in overseas wars.Twenty-four-year-old Wesley Sothole, who pleaded guilty, was handed a five-year suspended prison sentence and was ordered to be deported from South Africa.He is one of five Zimbabweans who were arrested at OR Tambo Airport in Johannesburg on 8 November. South African prosecutors have not confirmed which side the Zimbabweans allegedly intended to fight for.Sothole's four co-accused have yet to enter pleas and are due to return to the Kempton Park Magistrates' Court on 1 December for further plea and sentencing proceedings.Another four Zimbabweans were arrested at a hotel in Johannesburg at the same time in a joint operation and are facing a different court process.The investigation has involved South African police, Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies.South Africa's Foreign Military Assistance Act was passed in 1998 at a time when the government was concerned about members of the former apartheid security services going to fight elsewhere in Africa.There has been growing concern across Africa over the recruitment of its citizens to fight in the war in Ukraine, with some reportedly being lured to Russia by promises of lucrative civilian employment.A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.Some have been captured and are being held as prisoners of war.In March, Kenya estimated that 252 of its citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia. Kenyan Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue. He said an agreement had been reached for Russia to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.In the same month, Zimbabwe said that 15 of its nationals had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia in Ukraine, with more than 60 still trapped on the frontlines.The previous month, South Africa secured the return of 17 of its nationals who were allegedly tricked into joining the war. In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.South Africa's government said it condemned "the exploitation of young vulnerable people by individuals working with foreign military entities". Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.Additional reporting by Khanyisile Ngcobo in Johannesburg.

schema.headline: South African court convicts Zimbabwean of trying to fight in Russia-Ukraine war
